text: Every command so far has run from a terminal you installed and configured yourself. AWS CloudShell skips that setup entirely — it's a browser-based shell launched straight from the console, with nothing to install and nothing to configure.

A small terminal icon in the console's top navigation bar opens CloudShell in a small container. It's pre-authenticated, inheriting the same IAM permissions as whichever console user launched it, so there's no aws configure step and no access keys to manage. It's also pre-installed — the AWS CLI, Python, and other common tools are already there. CloudShell also gives each user 1 GB of persistent storage per Region, under $HOME, that survives between sessions, so a script you save today is still there next time.

Because the CLI is already configured, you can write and run a script the moment the shell opens. This one lists every S3 bucket and prints each one's object count and total size. aws s3 ls with no bucket name lists every bucket, one per line, with the name in the third column, so awk pulls that column out. The for loop runs once per bucket name, and inside it, aws s3 ls with --summarize lists that bucket's contents with a summary line, while tail -2 keeps just the total object count and total size instead of every object.

CloudShell is ideal for a quick, ad hoc task — checking something across every bucket, running a one-off command — without touching a local terminal. It has real limits: sessions time out after inactivity, and storage is capped at 1 GB per Region. It isn't meant for scheduled or unattended automation. A job that needs to run on a schedule belongs in a Lambda function or a CI/CD pipeline instead — CloudShell is for a human at the keyboard.

Scripts like this one often act on resources based on how they're labeled, not just what they're named. Lesson 20 covers tagging — attaching key-value metadata to AWS resources for organization, and for tracking exactly what each one costs.
